title: The Taste-Off
text:
<entity repo="place" guid="01a01887-b5f4-781c-8d38-122f7e1f38ba">The Loop</entity>'s third underlevel had its own ecology. A paper shop, a shuttered watch-repair, Vong's Dumpling Franchise #7 on the right under a red awning, and Mei's Dumplings on the left — no franchise, no awning, forty stolen inches of counter she'd annexed off the watch-repair's wall by leaning on it hard for years. The stationer's honest door sat dead center.

The two men stood in the middle with their backs to that door. Backs to <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>, in other words. A careless place to stand.

Vong was a compact sixty-year-old with the posture of a man who'd been taking bad news standing up for decades. The clipboard man wore a gray suit tailored to fit like a threat, and he held out a form the way a doctor holds out a chart. "—monthly insurance assessment. Standard for all food vendors on this underblock. The Tsui Group's protective services, standard rate—"

"Φ35 a week?" <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said from behind them, reading the figure upside-down. "Four hundred percent over the Meridian Merchant index. And your policy number's nine digits. <entity repo="place" guid="019d6143-a927-73ac-abfa-37c77f9cff8d">GLMZ</entity> policy numbers run eleven. That's somebody's neuretic handle on a form."

The clipboard man turned. He'd been in the work long enough to have stopped enjoying it. His face carried the apparatus of legitimacy — Tsui Group letterhead, a municipal seal, all of it official enough to survive a glance. "Not your stall."

"The coverage you've been operating under lapsed on the fourth," he went on, sliding his attention back to Vong. "Forty-two days ago. The protective license contingent on it is now void."

"Thirty-day grace period," Vong said, level. "Statute reads twenty-eight days left on the clock."

"The grace period applies to active licenses. Yours was lapsed. There's a distinction." He tapped the form without pointing at the number in section three. He didn't have to. Vong could see it from where he stood, and it was a number high enough to close the shop — high enough to make the calculation simple: pay the fraudulent claim, or spend six months in litigation nobody down here could afford.

"Go, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>," Vong said quietly. "This is mine to carry."

"I eat here," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. That was the whole of his position.

He'd half-expected the paperwork to end it. He pulled up the Tsui Group's public filing anyway — every collection franchise filed public or didn't operate — and it took under three minutes to find the part that mattered. The NeoCortex arranged the fields faster than conscious thought could follow: date, policy number, status.

"Your protective license lapsed," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, turning the screen. "The fourth. Not expired — lapsed. You've been writing paper on a dead license for eleven days. There's no reinstatement pending; the portal would show it."

The clipboard man looked at the screen for a long moment. He knew the number format. He knew what it meant. Not expired — lapsed — the difference between a renewal you'd missed and a standing you'd let die. Any form filed under it was a fraudulent document. Any Φ35 taken on it was restitution-eligible the second someone objected in the district record.

Then he handed the clipboard to his partner — the big one, the expensive shoes — and rolled his neck.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it as a man getting ready to leave. He was wrong.

"License is for the ones who pay clean," the clipboard man said. "Vong's not paying clean anymore. So this is the other visit." He looked at his partner. The big one didn't go for <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> — a professional, and professionals understand leverage. He came forward with the intention of making somebody stop being vertical, and he went for Vong's broth pot.

Forty liters of scalding pork-bone stock. A sixty-year-old man standing next to it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was moving before the big one's hand finished closing on the rim.

He didn't draw <entity repo="weapon" guid="019ed39c-6321-7c51-9691-f59b441b0bec">Silence</entity>. A drawn blade in an underlevel full of lunch customers was a conversation he'd have to finish, and this didn't need finishing. It needed interrupting. He crossed the three meters in the time it took the big one's shoulder to commit — the man hadn't lunged at the pot, he'd pivoted into it, shoulder-first, the kind of redirect that would tip forty liters of scalding stock across Vong's counter and Vong's legs in one smooth motion. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took the wrist off the rim — not a block, a redirect — and steered the shove ninety degrees into the franchise's steel prep counter. The stock rocked on its ring and held. One tongue of it slopped over the lip and hissed across the floor, where Vong had been standing half a second before. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s other hand had already moved him.

The big one came off the counter fast and threw the elbow. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> had left him the room to throw it. It caught <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> across the cheekbone — a real hit, a bright white line of pain, a mark by evening — and the cost bought the opening. Weight forward, lead knee proud. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> took the knee from the side with the flat of his boot. Not the joint. He'd walk with a limp for a week and tell the story straight; ruin the knee and he comes back, and he brings people. The big one folded into the spilled stock, swearing, done.

The clipboard man's hand went inside his jacket. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at him.

"<entity repo="weapon" guid="4ab24f74-61d4-4f45-b326-7c6b98c96279">Cacophony</entity> holds six," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. He hadn't drawn it. The sentence drew it. "You came to scald a sixty-year-old over Φ35 a week. Take your partner, take your dead license, and tell Marcus Tsui that Vong's block is documented now — times, faces, the shoes." A beat. "There's a kid on that roof who drew the shoes."

The hand came out empty. They hauled the big one up between them and left, tracking wet bootprints and the smell of spilled stock, and the underlevel breathed out. <entity repo="automaton" guid="019f04f1-58ed-77b6-b3b8-dd17d463bb34">The noodle vendor</entity>'s cheerful loop played on outside, indifferent.

Vong stood by his rescued pot with both hands flat on the counter. Steadying it, or himself.

"The tea stall on sub-two," he said. "Lin's. Forty years. She told them no, same as me. They didn't burn it. They just visited, and visited, and one week the customers decided sub-two wasn't worth the walk, and then Lin decided too. Now it's a jack kiosk and nobody remembers there was tea." His hands weren't quite steady. "That's how it's done now. Not a fire. An erasure. You wait for the block to forget."

"It's documented now," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "The next visit isn't a visit. It's a filing." He looked at the blood on his thumb without surprise. "Lin's mistake was being the only no on her block. You've got a whole block, Vong. Bill me for the dumplings I'm about to eat."

From his doorway, <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> made a small sound that was not a cough.

They came back at 14:00.

No clipboard this time. Three of them — the clipboard man, the big one moving carefully on his bad knee, and a third <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> hadn't seen before. Chrome thumb-rings, the flat affect of a man brought in for one purpose. The underlevel had thinned out after lunch. The third man's eyes went to Vong's counter first, then to the stairwell on the far wall, marking the ways out. That told <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> more than the chrome did.

"Marcus Tsui filed a complaint," the clipboard man said. He was talking to the room, not to any one person. "Assault of a licensed representative. Interference with contracted services. You've got a warrant flag running on your neuretics, <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity>. Check it if you want. We'll wait."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> didn't check it. A warrant flag cost sixty Φ to file and twenty to pull. It was a stall, not a threat. He also didn't move from where he stood, which was between the third man and Vong's pot.

"The complaint went to a licensing board that hasn't had a quorum since the fourth," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Same day your license lapsed. So the filing is stuck behind the lapse review. It's paperwork with nothing behind it. It dies the moment your reinstatement is denied, and it will be, because I've already sent the eleven-day gap documentation to <entity repo="faction" guid="019ee6a2-a172-7f5a-9451-03c4c3fe001b">the Office</entity> of Merchant Protections." He hadn't sent it yet. He was going to, in the next forty minutes, which was close enough. "You want to check THAT warrant, I'll wait."

The third man looked at the clipboard man. The clipboard man looked at his shoes.

The chrome rings were the tell. This one wasn't here for paper. He was here to stand in Vong's stall and let the afternoon customers see what they'd be walking into. He wouldn't touch Vong. He'd just be present, every afternoon, until keeping the franchise cost more than giving it up.

The same erasure Vong had described. Patient, and technically legal.

"Vong," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, without turning. "Is there a back entrance to this underlevel?"

"Loading dock. Service corridor, behind the watch-repair."

"The watch-repair's shuttered?"

"Three years."

"Whose lease?"

A pause. "Mine. I took it when they left. Cheaper than advertising."

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> looked at the third man. "You're standing in an extended franchise footprint. The loading dock, the service corridor, and the six feet of watch-repair wall all come off the same lease. You can stand here, but you're standing in his house. You want to tell Marcus Tsui you held a loitering position inside a vendor's licensed space, in front of witnesses, on the day I filed that lapse paperwork? That's intimidation after filing. Different charge. Higher one. They read it off a different shelf downtown."

The third man had the chrome rings and the flat affect and nothing else. He'd been hired for presence, not decisions. He looked at the clipboard man, who had been wrong about this block twice now.

They left.

Vong sat down on his prep stool and said nothing for a while. From the service corridor below, faint and steady, the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> ran its hum through the tiles — thirty meters down, Mach 6, the whole moving world.

"Every time I tell them no," Vong said, "I think about Lin."

"You're not Lin," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said. "Lin didn't have the service corridor and a kid on the roof and a <entity repo="vocabulary" guid="019d6143-aafb-7b6b-bcbc-b8614f9d228f">samurai</entity> who eats here on Tuesdays."

He went upstairs and filed the documentation.

The Office of Merchant Protections portal loaded slow, the way it always did, a public docket built to discourage the people it was meant to protect. The form was the same every time: date, location, names if available, what happened, who witnessed it. He typed Vong's block number. Uploaded the screenshot of the dead license — no reinstatement pending, eleven days of nothing where a credential should have been. He filled the witness line: six lunch customers who'd confirm it if asked, and <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity>, who'd drawn the big one's shoes off the rooftop log while <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was still reading the clipboard. That was the leverage. Not the violence. The paperwork. You broke the paperwork, you broke the system's claim to anything.

The filing cost Φ8.50. He paid it from his personal account and hit submit.

The confirmation code populated — a case number, a line drawn in the underlevel's invisible architecture that said Vong's block was not erasable, not this week, not without leaving a mark someone downtown could read. A small stone set in a current, changing nothing except the angle at which the water fell.

He wrote the number on the back of a receipt — <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s paper, because <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity>'s paper had weight — and went back down to leave it on Vong's counter.

By 14:00 there was a chalk line on the floor. By 15:30 there were two, with a disputed strip between them and three customers eating in the gap, braced to be told to pick a side.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was at Mei's — he alternated weeks, had for six years, and both owners knew it — with a cut cheek and a late lunch when <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> came down the stairs. Somebody had sent for her. She came down the way a woman does when she's been handed a job beneath her skill and above her patience, carrying a wooden spoon she hadn't put down before leaving her own counter. She stopped on the neutral chalk and let the quiet do half the work.

"Both of you have sold dumplings down here longer than half these buildings have stood," she said. "You've both overcharged me. I paid, because the food was worth it." She looked at the two lines, then at the three customers wedged in the gap between them. "I'm not an arbitrator. I'm a customer owed better than this."

"You're the only one on this block both stalls will hear," Vong said.

"You started it," Mei said.

"The awning—"

"The broth pot—"

"The awning was over the line by a hand," <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-3404-79c2-a8f6-2942f504698e">Mrs. Chen</entity> said, without turning to either of them. "The broth pot's been in that corner since before the strip mattered. I know because I've been paying you both to feed me since the year the water came up to the second level. That's not a claim I made lightly and it's not one you'll argue." She tapped the spoon once against her palm. "A block runs on people who don't ask each other for receipts. You've made everyone down here reach for a wallet twice — once for the food, once to guess whose side of the chalk they're standing on. That's the part I won't pay."

She turned to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. She didn't ask. She had spent seventy years not asking for things, and the not-asking was the request. He finished his dumpling and stood up. His cheek had stiffened to a dull throb that woke when he chewed. A fair price, for an afternoon that had twice nearly cost Vong his hands.

The taste-off was <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity>'s idea, and the speed with which the logbook made it official suggested it had been everyone's idea at once.

DUMPLING COMMISSION: OFFICIAL RECORD. CHAIR: MR. KYLE (VISIBLE INJURY, SEE 11:40 ENTRY). RECORDER: RAFTERS. PANEL: DENTS, BOOST. OBJECTIVE: BETTER DUMPLING, FOR BLOCK PEACE. NOTE: BOSS GOT HIT TODAY. ONCE. WE LOGGED IT. THIS LOG IS HONEST.

Both stalls cooked. Vong ran his standard pork-and-chive — thicker wrap, machine-even pleating, corners sealed with the precision of someone who'd done it ten thousand times, every inspection star it had ever earned. Mei brought the original: thinner wrap, hand-crimped in a pattern <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity> sketched in the margin for the record, ginger-forward with something older underneath. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> ate four of each. Vong's wrapper held the filling's heat longer; Mei's broth was cleaner, the salt distributed so it didn't land all at once on the tongue. Different choices. Different hands. The cut in his cheek woke at every one of Mei's. He took that as evidence of the ginger and kept it out of the minutes.

The crew filed scorecards, from TWO POINTS AND A STAR up to a drawing of a thumbs-up with a Φ1 price tag. A crowd had gathered — chalk lines and official proceedings will do that, word moving through the underlevel the way it does, *taste-off, somebody's going to lose* — and <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> had migrated from his doorway to the building's first inside window for the better angle.

<entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-04fb-7227-94d9-6b4d889ce52b">Boost</entity> tallied the cards twice, then a third time, her pencil going slower each pass. When he finally turned the logbook around, the count was a dead tie — and every one of Vong's points, <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> saw, was clustered on the crew's own cards. The neutral crowd, the strangers who'd wandered in off the chalk lines, had scored Mei's to a person. Vong saw it the same instant <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> did.

He set down his ladle. Wiped his hands with great deliberation. And said to the whole gathered block that a rigged panel of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s own people wasn't a taste-off, it was theater — that he'd had to prove he was better, and instead a room of <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s crew had proved they were the same — and he'd take the real verdict, the crowd's, as proof the Commission had picked its winner before the first dumpling hit the water.

"A tie is a loss for me," he said. Flat, the way accusations come out when the accuser already knows the words won't stop. Half the crowd murmured agreement. The line was already re-forming on Mei's side of the chalk, feet voting where scorecards hadn't been trusted to.

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity>' pen stopped over the honest log with nothing fair left to write, and the block peace the whole thing was supposed to buy was now visibly worse than when they'd started.

"For the record," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> said, to the chalk and the crowd and both owners, "Vong's franchise makes a technically excellent dumpling. Consistent. Well-priced. You know exactly what you get, any day of any week." Vong nodded with professional dignity. "Mei's original is better."

Mei made a sound that was not quite a sound. Vong's jaw went through an expression and out the far side.

"By a margin that doesn't justify a chalk line," <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> went on, over the crowd's murmur. "Vong, your guarantee covers the gap — inspection rating, delivery network, the app. Mei's got seventeen years of recipe folded by hand. Two stalls, two reasons to buy a dumpling. You're both leaving money on the floor fighting over an inch." He let that sit. Then he said the part that was the actual point. "This afternoon Marcus Tsui sent three men to stand in Vong's stall and wait for the foot traffic to decide it wasn't worth the walk. They left because the paperwork went in and the stall had footage to stand on. That changes nothing about next week, or the week after, or Lin's tea stall on sub-two that's a jack kiosk now and will never be tea again." He looked at both of them. "A block with one stall is a block that can be made to forget it. A block with two stalls arguing about awnings at lunch is a block that's LOUD. People come to it on purpose. You two are each other's insurance, and you've been drawing a chalk line down the middle of it."

He looked at <entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity>. "That how the minutes read?"

<entity repo="character" guid="01a0030b-6067-735a-8326-4aff028cb856">Rafters</entity> consulted the logbook with the gravity of a senior analyst. "Exactly how they read. I can charge for certified copies."

The chalk was gone by 16:30. Vong sent one complimentary order of pork-and-chive to Mei's counter without a word; Mei took it without a word. Closest the underlevel had come to a diplomatic event in twenty years. Vong put the franchise testimonial card in his window — cheap stock, the kind that yellowed in a month, printed on the same run as the inspection rating so the ink matched. Beside it he set a second card, hand-lettered, that hadn't been there this morning, the letters pressed hard enough to leave indents on the back: BEST ORIGINAL ON THE BLOCK — SEE MEI, NEXT COUNTER. He positioned it to catch the afternoon light coming down the stairwell, where the foot traffic from street level would read it before it read anything else. Insurance, posted where the block could read it.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> was leaving at 17:20 when <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> opened his door the particular width of a man who'd been saving something all day.

"Come in. The occasion warrants the good shelf." Inside, the labeled drawers sat in their brown-inked rows, dates running back forty years, indexed by a system nobody but <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> could read. He poured without asking and pushed the cup handle-first. "The Tsui Group isn't my clientele — impersonation filings are public, and I don't sell what I can read for free." He settled onto his stool. "I watched the whole thing. Morning and afternoon. The license. The pot. The chrome thumb-rings." His eyes went, briefly, to <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>'s cheek. "The interruptions, plural."

"You watched a man go for a sixty-year-old and made tea?"

"I sell maps, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. I don't walk the territory. A stationer who picks up a weapon is a stationer no one trusts with a secret again." He said it without apology. "But I noticed you didn't draw the sword. A man went for Vong's pot — twice, two different ways — and you put them down with paperwork and a boot and a sentence. The leverage was real. The filing was real. The sub-two corridor was real. Three kinds of paper and one measured piece of violence, in order." He polished his glasses. "The Tsui Group needed a reason to stop. The stalls needed a verdict. Your standing client needed" — the smallest brightness — "a dumpling methodology, apparently."

He turned back to his desk, where three forms sat stamped and dated in that small, precise hand. "There are two kinds of people who last in a place like this. The ones who don't move unless the contract says to move, and the ones who move and then write the paper to cover what they've already done. I'm the first. You're the second. That's why your afternoon holds up and mine only records it." He dipped his pen. "Two stalls arguing is noise, Mr. <entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity>. One stall is silence, and silence is what makes a block disappear off the district roll. You kept the noise. That was the work. Don't tell me it was an accident."

"Don't."

He said it about all of it, and <entity repo="character" guid="019f441d-1ab1-78dc-bbb2-58870428613d">Vey</entity> — who understood the word the way he understood filings — didn't press.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> drank the tea, which was from the good shelf, and set the cup down square.

The terminal chirped on his way to the stairs.

STANDING CONTRACT — AMENDMENT. CLIENT HAS REVIEWED TODAY. CLIENT NOTES: THE INJURY WAS AVOIDABLE IF THE ENGINEER'S DRONE PROPOSAL (FILED, DECLINED) HAD BEEN ADOPTED.
CLIENT HAS RE-FILED THE PROPOSAL.
GRATUITY: Φ0.5 — ITEMIZED: THE CHEEK. ADDENDUM: CLIENT NOTED THE CHEEK AT 14:40.
CLIENT DISLIKES THE CHEEK.

<entity repo="character" guid="019d6143-a648-7876-9688-0f6d38d70075">Kyle</entity> read it twice on the stairs. The gratuity wasn't payment — Φ0.5 was insulting as payment. It was a record, logged so a street cut became a documented injury that might one day bear on his ability to work. Corpo files didn't care about a man bleeding in a stall. They cared about the same blood once it had a line item.

The cut was stiffening, tight enough now that turning his head pulled at it, and behind him the underlevel settled into its evening — Vong's closing sequence, Mei's last fold, the <entity repo="corponation" guid="0d831459-182f-4efc-9920-bdf9e032c61d">Pulse</entity> dragging its Mach-6 tremor through the floor thirty meters down. He decided the client could dislike the cheek all it wanted. A cut cheek was cheap. Vong still had his hands.
